title: Slotting + Tail-Chop Emulation: Field Diary and Results
content:
Summary:

Field diary of a week-long probe into how slot-based batch formation (slotting) interacts with short, high-concurrency microbursts that produce 'tail-chop' behavior: many small bursts that repeatedly preempt in-flight batches and cause P99+/P99.9 regression. Goal was to reproduce, quantify, and propose mitigations for tail-latency regressions while preserving throughput and fairness across tenant priority classes.

Motivation / Background:
- Several customer incidents (INF-2345) show P99.9 spikes under bursty traffic even when average latency and throughput are healthy.
- Hypothesis: slotting (assigning requests to time slots to avoid head-of-line blocking) reduces average queueing but creates deterministic flush points that can be repeatedly preempted by high-priority microbursts, producing many short-lived batches (tail-chop).
- Secondary hypothesis: interactions with KV cache eviction (short-lived batches bypassing cache warmups) amplifies tail quantiles.

Experiment scope and constraints:
- Hardware: 8x A100s per test cluster, single-node experiments to isolate scheduling; small multi-node experiment for routing/fallback checks.
- Models: gpt-small-opt-3b (decoder-only), seq-len distributions: 64/256/1024 mixture to emulate product workloads.
- Synthetic traces: two sources
  * microburst-mix: 90% short (<=64 tokens), 10% long (>=512) at high concurrency spikes (50 reqs/sec spikes sustained 3s), repeated every 20s
  * telemetered-prod-trace: 30m of sampled production traffic (anonymized) used as baseline
- Metrics collected: P50/P90/P95/P99/P99.9 latencies, batch size distribution, flush counts, preemption counts, KV cache hit rate, tokens/sec, GPU occupancy, and per-request CPU wait time.
- Baseline scheduler: dynamic-window + opportunistic slotting disabled. Experiments test pure-slotting, slotting+grace, slotting+preemption-quarantine, and hybrid time-size flush heuristics.

Methodology / Controls:
1) Warmup: 10-minute steady-state run of telemetered-prod-trace to warm KV caches and kernels.
2) Run microburst-mix for 30 minutes under each scheduler variant. Capture full traces.
3) Repeat runs (n=5) per variant to capture variability; shuffle random seeds for arrival jitter.
4) Ensure identical model weights, no autoscaling, identical batch op kernels.
5) Use per-tenant priority classes: normal, business, internal. Measure fairness by relative latency uplift and throughput share.

Scheduler Variants Tested:
- S0 (Baseline): dynamic-window, flush-on-timeout, opportunistic small-batch allowance.
- S1 (Pure-slot): fixed slot length 50ms, flush-on-slot-boundary only, no timeouts inside slot.
- S2 (Slot+grace): slot length 50ms, but requests older than 20ms in a slot can trigger early flush (grace threshold).
- S3 (Slot+quarantine): slot length 50ms, but preempted batches enter a short quarantine period (100ms) where they cannot be rebatched with high-priority arrivals; aims to reduce churn.
- S4 (Hybrid size-time): slot length 50ms, but size threshold 16 tokens triggers immediate flush regardless of slot boundary.

Representative commands used (for reproducibility):
- workload generator: "./bin/regen_trace --trace microburst-mix.json --rate 600 --seed 42"
- scheduler toggle: "/bin/serving-runtime --scheduler=slot --slot-ms=50 --grace-ms=20 --quarantine-ms=100"
- metrics extraction: "python tools/latency_agg.py --in /tmp/trace.json --out /tmp/agg.csv"

Key Results (aggregated across n=5 runs, microburst-mix):
- S0 Baseline: P99=280ms, P99.9=620ms, median batch size=10, preemptions/sec=0.8, KV-hit=0.72
- S1 Pure-slot: P99=320ms (+14%), P99.9=980ms (+58%), median batch size=12, preemptions/sec=4.6, KV-hit=0.45
- S2 Slot+grace: P99=290ms (+3%), P99.9=660ms (+6%), median batch size=11, preemptions/sec=1.6, KV-hit=0.68
- S3 Slot+quarantine: P99=305ms (+9%), P99.9=420ms (-32%), median batch size=11, preemptions/sec=1.2, KV-hit=0.70
- S4 Hybrid size-time: P99=275ms (-2%), P99.9=480ms (-22%), median batch size=14, preemptions/sec=0.9, KV-hit=0.75

Immediate observations and interpretation:
- Pure-slotting (S1) produced the worst tail (P99.9) due to repeated preemption of slot-bound batches by concentrated spikes. Preemptions/sec jumped ~5x and KV hit rate collapsed as batches became too small/short-lived to amortize caching benefits.
- Adding a small grace window (S2) recovered most of the baseline tail behavior while preserving some of the batching benefits of slotting. Grace lets slightly older requests force a flush so they don't keep getting delayed into subsequent preempted slots.
- Quarantine (S3) strongly reduced P99.9 relative to S1, better than S2 for extreme tails. Hypothesis: preventing immediate rebatching after preemption avoids pathological churn where a high-priority spike causes many tiny batches in quick succession. However, quarantine slightly increased median and P99 compared to baseline because it delays some reprocessing.
- Hybrid size-time flush (S4) gave the best overall balance: slightly improved median, big improvement in P99.9 vs S1 and S0. Larger median batch size and higher KV-hit show that size-driven flushes help amortize kernel and cache costs even under slotting.

Additional profiling notes (trace excerpts):
- Example trace snippet (timestamp, slot_id, req_id, action):
  13:02:14.092, slot-42, r-5311, received
  13:02:14.107, slot-42, r-5312, received
  13:02:14.120, slot-42, r-5313, flush-initiated (slot-boundary)
  13:02:14.121, kworker0, batch-exec r-5311..5313, preempted-by r-5400 (high-prio)
  13:02:14.125, r-5311, restarted, cache-miss
- KV cache traces indicate repeated short-lived write/read cycles; small-batch churn correlates with ~40% lower GPU kernel occupancy for S1 runs.
- GPU profiles showed stalls linked to CPU-side batching decisions: excessive syscalls for scheduling and preemption bookkeeping during microbursts.

Fairness observations (per-tenant):
- Under S1, high-priority tenants achieved low latency but at severe cost to normal tenants (P99.9 normal tenants increased by 2.7x).
- S3 quarantine preserved better fairness: high-priority still gets preferential latency but normal tenants had fewer catastrophic outliers.
- S4 hybrid kept throughput shares stable across classes while minimizing tail impact.

Root causes distilled:
1) Deterministic flush boundaries without adaptive escape (pure-slot) cause repeated preemption cycles under bursty high-priority arrivals.
2) Small, preempted batches hurt KV cache warmups and kernel amortization, magnifying tail quantiles.
3) Preemption bookkeeping on CPU path becomes a new bottleneck when preemptions/sec > ~3s, increasing jitter.

Mitigations tested and recommended changes (practical / incremental):
- Short-term (deployable as a flag): enable hybrid size-time flush by default for slotting-enabled fleets. Flag: --slot-hybrid=true, --slot-min-size=12
- Medium-term: implement 'preemption quarantine' policy as a tunable option per-tenant to avoid immediate rebatching of preempted requests (configurable ms).
- Long-term: refactor preemption bookkeeping to reduce syscalls (batch preemption updates instead of per-request) and integrate KV cache warm-start heuristics so recently preempted requests retain cache pointers for a short TTL.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Sensitivity across model families: we only tested one model. Does hybrid help equally for decoder-only 7b and 70b-like memory-bound models? Need follow-up runs.
- Autoscale interactions: when cluster autoscaling is in play, slotting dynamics might change. Schedule a mixed-run with Dedicated-mode autoscaler.
- Production telemetry: propose adding a derived metric 'preemptions_per_1k_reqs' and alert if > 1.5x baseline.

Immediate action items (owners):
- Diego: implement quick hybrid flag PR and perf test (due 2025-12-08).
- Priya: run S4 on 7b model and report by 2025-12-12.
- Noah: prototype batched preemption bookkeeping change and microbench for syscall reduction (due 2025-12-15).
- Maya: add preemptions_per_1k_reqs metric to observability and create dashboard (due 2025-12-05).

Notes to self / rough brainstorm:
- Could we exploit prefix-key affinity to reduce cold-KV misses when preemptions occur? Maybe tag requests with ephemeral affinity id for 200ms.
- Consider per-tenant grace thresholds tuned by SLA class (internal low SLAs get shorter grace).
